### 4. Canon EOS R5 Mark II
It feels criminal to rank the Canon R5 Mark II outside of the top three, but that’s just a testament to how impressive cameras are today. The EOS R5 II is a high-resolution, high-speed beast that’s equally capable of landscape photography and sports/wildlife. In that sense, it’s pretty similar to the three cameras above.
The Canon EOS R5 II has a 45-megapixel sensor and can shoot a whopping 30 FPS. It has an excellent autofocus system, and like the three cameras above, it can also shoot 8K video – in this case at a highly impressive 60p. Canon found a way to push a ton of data through the EOS R5’s pipeline, and it makes this camera excellent for action photography and video in addition to its high quality for landscapes.
As you would expect, all of this comes at a high price: the EOS R5 II costs $4400 body only. (Check the price, though; it goes on sale pretty often.) If you can’t find a good deal on the EOS R5 Mark II, the good news is that you can get the previous generation Canon EOS R5 for a more reasonable price around $3300, and we’ve even seen it on sale as low as $2600. Compared to the “Mark II,” the original EOS R5 is surprisingly similar – a tad slower, but still blazing fast, and it has the same 45-megapixel sensor. If I were including older generation cameras in this list, I could easily rank the original EOS R5 right below the Mark II.
Canon EOS R5 Mark II + RF14-35mm F4 L IS USM @ 14mm, ISO 100, 6 seconds, f/16.0

### 5. Sony A7r V
Almost reaching the lofty heights of the Sony A1 II, yet more than $2500 cheaper, is the Sony A7r V. It sells for $4200 (check price) and has an even higher-resolution 61-megapixel sensor.
The A7r V still manages to shoot at 10 FPS despite the high-res sensor, and it has a huge buffer of 583 images. And the autofocus system is incredible: It uses Sony’s newest artificial intelligence, subject-recognition algorithms. Cutting through the buzzwords, this means the A7r V can recognize subjects like birds and people even when they face away from the camera or have an unusual pose.
For a lot of photographers who are considering the Nikon Z9 or Sony A1 II, the A7R V will actually make more sense. It’s an excellent camera for landscape photography because of the high-res sensor, and at 10 FPS, it’s still great for photographing wildlife, too. It doesn’t quite reach the maximum specifications of either the Z9 or A1, but for most applications, it will do just as well as either of those cameras.
Sony A7R III + FE 24-105mm F4 G OSS @ 29mm, ISO 100, 1 second, f/11.0

### 6. Canon EOS R1 and EOS R3
If you want a more specialized camera for sports and wildlife photography, it’s hard to beat the Canon EOS R1, or its little brother the R3. Unlike the previous cameras on this list, the EOS R1 and EOS R3 don’t have a 40+ megapixel sensor; instead, they’re “only” 24 megapixels. But these two cameras can shoot more than 30 FPS with a functionally unlimited buffer. They also have Canon’s unique “eye-sensing autofocus” that begins focusing at the spot _you look at in the composition_. It’s a seriously cool feature.
I paired the two cameras into one entry on this list because they’re surprisingly similar. The main benefits of the EOS R1 are 40 FPS rather than 30 FPS, and a pre-release burst mode. Given that the prices are $6800 and $5400 respectively, I frankly think that a lot of photographers should go with the EOS R3 instead. But if you find pre-release RAW to be worth the extra cash, then of course the flagship EOS R1 has the advantage.
For any fast-paced genres of photography, you’ll want to take a long look at these two cameras. If you don’t need the high-res sensors of the Nikon Z9, Sony A1 II, Sony A7r V, or Canon EOS R5 II, it equals or beats all of them in performance and gives you smaller, more manageable files.

### 7. Sony A7 V
It’s crazy that I haven’t gotten to talk about the Sony A7 V yet – one of the best all-around mirrorless cameras that you can get today, and a great deal, too.
This $2900 camera (check price) has a 33-megapixel sensor, which is a sweet spot for both landscape and wildlife photography. At 30 FPS blackout-free shooting, and borrowing its autofocus system from the Sony A1, it’s an incredible choice for fast-moving action.
Sony has the advantage of being in the full-frame mirrorless market longer than Nikon or Canon, and it’s starting to show now that we’re on the 5th generation of the A7. For example, the large lens lineup for Sony mirrorless cameras (including third-party autofocus lenses) gives you more choices than Canon or Nikon, even though those two companies are catching up.
One of the best “under the radar” features of the Sony A7 V is that it has the redesigned menu system found on Sony’s newest cameras (including the A1 and A7r V). Frankly, Sony’s old menu was a pain to use, even once you got used to it. The new menu makes the camera much more usable.
Sony a7 V + FE 400-800mm F6.3-8 G OSS @ 400mm, ISO 100, 1/250, f/8.0

### 8. Sony A9 III
The Sony A9 III presents entirely new possibilities with its 24-megapixel global shutter. This single innovation completely eliminates rolling shutter and allows flash photography to work at all shutter speeds without high-speed sync.
Due to its new shutter technology, it has an incredible 1/80,000 minimum shutter speed and can shoot at 120fps. It seems very unlikely that anything in the normal world will be too fast for this camera.
At $6000, the Sony A9 III is arguably overpriced, and many of the other cameras here will beat it for other applications – i.e., anything other than sports. This is definitely a highly specialized camera. Still, if you’re aching to use a global shutter, there’s no other camera on this list _but_ the Sony A9III.
Official Sample Shot: the Sony a9III allows flash to be used at all shutter speeds without high-speed sync. ILCE-9M3 + FE 24-70mm F2.8 GM II @ 53mm, ISO 400, 1/6400, f/8.0

### 9. Canon EOS R6 Mark III
Alongside the Sony A7 V, one of the best mirrorless cameras today in terms of price-vs-features is the Canon EOS R6 Mark III. This camera is a replacement for the prior generation EOS R6 Mark II that also remains an excellent choice.
The EOS R6 III has a 32.5-megapixel sensor (compared to 24 megapixels on the previous R6 II).It shoots up to 40 FPS stills, has dual memory card slots, and uses Canon’s superb dual-pixel mirrorless autofocus system. Unlike the previous generation – and unlike most of the other cameras on this list – it’s capable of shooting 7K RAW video.
It does all this at a starting price of $2800. The prior generation EOS R6 Mark II has many of the same features (though a 24 megapixel sensor) and is going on sale for cheap prices these days – about $2000 if it’s on sale.
The EOS R6 Mark III and even the Mark II are practically as good as the Nikon Z9, Sony A1 II, Canon R5 II, and other top cameras where autofocus is concerned. Well done to Canon for putting such a good autofocus system on a less expensive camera. That said, if you’re mainly interested in landscape or studio photography and don’t need so many action photography features, you’d probably happier with one of the other cameras on this list.
Canon EOS R6 + RF800mm F11 IS STM @ 800mm, ISO 1600, 1/1000, f/11.0

### 10. Nikon Z6 III
Nikon has really outdone themselves on the Z6 III, giving this affordable camera essentially the same autofocus system and other features as the top-end Nikon Z9 and Nikon Z8. The main drawback is simply the lower resolution sensor – at 24 megapixels, it’s a little on the low side for today’s world, although still plenty for reasonably sized prints.
The Nikon Z6 III is one of the least expensive ways to get pro-level autofocus and viewfinder performance. As you can see in our comparison of the Nikon Z8 vs the Nikon Z6 III, it even beats the more expensive cameras in a few areas. Not bad for a $2700 camera (and one that often goes on sale for $2300).
NIKON Z6 III + NIKKOR Z 100-400mm f/4.5-5.6 VR S @ 400mm, ISO 180, 1/1000, f/6.3

### 11. Fuji GFX-100S II
One of the most specialized mirrorless cameras today is the Fuji GFX-100S. It’s not a sports or wildlife photography camera at all – instead, it’s a 100-megapixel medium format beast. For landscape photography, architecture, product photography, or other high-resolution needs, it’s probably the best camera on this list. For nonmoving subjects, it even has a sensor-shift mode to quadruple the resolution to 400 megapixels!
My main landscape cameras for years have been the Fuji GFX cameras, and I love them. The lenses, image quality, and dynamic range are amazing, and once you go to medium format, you won’t go back. But because of how specialized this camera is, I don’t think it makes sense to rank the GFX-100S above some of the more practical cameras on this list.
I give a lot of credit to Fuji for releasing the GFX-100S at a reasonable price (for medium format) of $5700. That puts the camera within line of the Nikon Z9 and Sony A1. Even though the GFX-100S is a much slower-paced camera, it has the best sensor of the three.
GFX100S + GF32-64mmF4 R LM WR @ 64mm, ISO 100, 60 seconds, f/16.0. © Meg Faehl

### 12.Fuji GFX-50S II
Pretty much everything that I said about the GFX-100S II above also applies to its little brother, the GFX-50S II. The two cameras share the same design, both have IBIS, and both match each other in most specifications.
However, “most” specifications is not “all” specifications. The GFX-50S II has a 50-megapixel sensor rather than 100-megapixel sensor, and it has a slower contrast-detect autofocus system. The GFX-50S II is also limited to 1080p video for some reason, while the GFX-100S shoots 4K.
Will these differences matter to the typical medium format shooter? Most of them probably won’t, but the sensor resolution might. Considering that the GFX-50S II costs $4000, it’s a pretty stellar deal for medium format. However, if your main reason for getting into this system is maximum detail, you may have a sneaking desire to go with the 100-megapixel version.
GFX 50S + GF32-64mmF4 R LM WR @ 53.6mm, ISO 100, 1/200, f/5.6

### 13. Nikon Z5 II
One of the best values on this entire list is the Nikon Z5 II. Despite being a full-frame camera with plenty of advanced features, including an autofocus system that practically matches that of the Nikon Z8 and Z9, I’ve seen it go as low as $1600 new (check current sales).
You might think that a $1600 full-frame camera (okay, $1850 when it’s not on sale) would have some major flaws, but the Z5 would prove you wrong. Its 24 megapixel sensor is very good, the camera has dual memory card slots, and it still includes in-body image stabilization.
It’s pretty much a “Z6 III lite” and only loses at the margins: 15 FPS rather than 20, a 12-second buffer rather than unlimited, no 6K video, and a less advanced viewfinder. (See the full Z5 II vs Z6 III comparison here.) These are nice features, but none of them are essential to most photographers. If you’re on a budget, it’s hard to beat the Nikon Z5 II – although I will point out that the previous generation Z5 is about the cheapest possible full-frame mirrorless camera, especially if bought used, and it’s a solid camera if you don’t need a top-notch AF system.
NIKON Z 5 + NIKKOR Z 24-200mm f/4-6.3 VR @ 27mm, ISO 100, 1/125, f/8.0

### 14. Nikon Zf
The Nikon Zf is a retro-themed mirrorless camera that pretty much matches the Nikon Z5 II in feature set. The main difference is the design of the camera (and a slightly higher price for the Zf). It’s hard to deny that this is a beautiful camera:
Between the Zf and the Z5 II, the main differences are slightly better battery life on the Zf and slightly better video features on the Z5 II. The price of the Zf is $2200, though – $350 higher than that of the Z5 II, at least when it’s not on sale. It’s probably a camera that you buy more for the ergonomics and beautiful design, while you’d buy the Z5 II if those things are less important than the price. But you can see more at our Zf vs Z5 II comparison to figure out if any of the small differences matter to you.

### 15. Panasonic S5 II
One area where Panasonic had been lagging behind the best mirrorless cameras from Nikon, Canon, and Sony was autofocus performance (at least in Panasonic’s full-frame cameras). The Panasonic S5 II fixes this by introducing the company’s phase-detect AF.
Although the S5 II has a 24-megapixel sensor, don’t let that fool you if you’re a landscape photographer. Like some of the Sony and Fuji cameras on this list, the Panasonic S5 II has a high-resolution pixel-shift mode that quadruples a photo’s resolution to 96 megapixels! This only works if the subject is staying still, but I found that it produces fairly natural results in previous Panasonic mirrorless cameras, like the Panasonic S1R (see our review).
The Panasonic S5 II also has some very good video features, capturing up to 6K video internally. It even has a dedicated cooling fan to allow the camera to keep filming for long stretches without overheating. Add that to the 200-image RAW buffer, the 30 FPS shooting, and the $2000 price, and you have a very versatile mirrorless camera indeed.
DC-S1R + LUMIX S 24-105/F4 @ 105mm, ISO 200, 1/1, f/5.0

### 16. Nikon Z7 II
If you want a high-resolution camera that’s excellent for landscape photography, you should look closely at the 45 megapixel, $3000 Nikon Z7 II.
Even though the Nikon Z7 II isn’t as fast as some other mirrorless cameras – including most of Nikon’s other cameras – it would be one of my top few choices on the market for landscape photography. An unsung feature of the Nikon Z7 II is the base ISO of 64, giving it dynamic range that rivals even medium format! Not to mention that the Z lenses are some of the sharpest lenses of all time, making it an ideal system to capture a lot of detail without weighing very much.
When the Nikon Z7 II was released, it got some bad press for the autofocus system’s wildlife photography capabilities. Of course, it’s all relative: I found that even the previous generation Z7 was perfectly fine for fast wildlife once you get the hang of it. But it’s true that you’d be better served with something like the Canon EOS R5 II, Sony A7r V, or Nikon Z8 if wildlife photography is a priority for you.
NIKON Z 7 II + NIKKOR Z 14-24mm f/2.8 S @ 24mm, ISO 64, 2.5 seconds, f/11.0

### 17. Fujifilm X-T5
I’m a big fan of Fuji’s mirrorless cameras, and the X-T5 has some of the company’s best features so far.
With its 40-megapixel X-Trans sensor capable of producing excellent image quality, in-body image stabilization, a fast X-Processor 4 with Quad CPU that is capable of pushing up 6K video, F-Log gamma for extended dynamic range when shooting video, long battery life, an insanely fast and accurate autofocus system, and a bright 3.69 million dot EVF, the Fuji X-T3 is an impressive stills and video camera. It even shoots 15 FPS (20 FPS if you don’t mind a 1.3x crop), making it a good camera for sports and wildlife, too.
While it is an exceptionally good camera in many ways, it is still an APS-C sensor camera, so it doesn’t do as well at high ISOs or shallow depth of field as the other cameras on this list. It’s also more expensive than most APS-C cameras at $1700 (check price and availability). You may want to consider the prior generation X-T4, too, which I’ve seen go on sale now that the X-T5 is out.
Captured with Fuji X-T4 + XF 23mmF2 R WR @ 23mm, ISO 160, 0.6 sec, f/5.6

### 18. Fujifilm X-H2S
If you want speed in a crop-sensor camera, the Fuji X-H2S is for you. It has a stacked 26MP sensor, which is plenty of resolution for most situations. And it’s _fast_.
Thanks to the camera’s stacked BSI sensor, it can shoot RAW photos at 40 FPS. At that frame rate, your buffer is still a very reasonable 140 images. Drop the burst down to 15 FPS, and you’ll get a 1000-image buffer. So, to say that this camera is good for fast action is an understatement.
The X-H2S also has some very impressive video features with excellent-quality footage – not only with 4K120 but also with 6K 30p. Between this camera and the X-T5 above, I consider the X-T5 more versatile because of its higher-resolution sensor, but the X-H2S isn’t far behind.

### 19. Canon EOS R7
Another fast, APS-C camera that has been turning a lot of heads is the Canon EOS R7. At $1500, it’s about $1000 less expensive than the Fuji X-H2S while nipping at its heels in terms of features.
Those features begin with a 32.5-megapixel sensor, which is high for an APS-C camera. The EOS R7 has a 30 FPS burst, 4K 60p filming, in-body image stabilization, and a great autofocus system. It also has one of my favorite features, a pre-release burst mode that allows you to record photos up to 1/2 second before you’ve fully pressed the shutter button. This is great for unpredictable wildlife photography.
One potential issue is that the buffer is not as big as that of the Fuji X-H2S. The Canon EOS R7 gives you 93 shots at 30 FPS and 187 shots at 15 FPS (assuming that you’re using lossless compressed CRAW). These figures are not low, but not best-in-class either. Even so,the EOS R7 would be one of my first choices for sports and wildlife photography on a budget today.

### 20. Nikon Z50 II
Nikon’s attempt at a high-speed APS-C camera is the Z50 II, and it’s a very good camera in many ways. The autofocus system is borrowed from the flagship Nikon Z9, so it’s a highly capable camera for sports and wildlife photography.
The main downside of this camera is the 20 megapixel resolution – tied for the lowest on this list. 20 megapixels is still plenty for most prints, but it doesn’t leave as much room for cropping, and in today’s world, a lot of people would prefer something over 30 MP just in case they’re making large prints.
Still, the price is good (around $1000) and the features are very impressive. This camera could be an excellent choice depending on your priorities.
NIKON Z50_2 + NIKKOR Z 180-600mm f/5.6-6.3 VR @ 600mm, ISO 25600, 1/250, f/6.3

### 21. Canon EOS R8
This 24-megapixel, full-frame mirrorless camera is aimed at a budget-conscious audience (at least among full-frame cameras) with a price of $1500. It sometimes goes on sale for less; check the current price).
Benefits of the EOS R8 include 40 FPS shooting (electronic shutter) and Canon’s pre-release shutter mode. A drawback of this camera is that it doesn’t have in-body image stabilization, and it has just a single SD card slot. Still, these compromises are what allowed Canon to keep the price of the EOS R8 relatively low. It’s still a great camera with impressive bang for your buck.

The Canon EOS R5 II has a 45-megapixel sensor and can shoot a whopping 30 FPS. It has an excellent autofocus system, and like the three cameras above, it can also shoot 8K video – in this case at a highly impressive 60p. Canon found a way to push a ton of data through the EOS R5’s pipeline, and it makes this camera excellent for action photography and video in addition to its high quality for landscapes.
As you would expect, all of this comes at a high price: the EOS R5 II costs $4400 body only. (Check the price, though; it goes on sale pretty often.) If you can’t find a good deal on the EOS R5 Mark II, the good news is that you can get the previous generation Canon EOS R5 for a more reasonable price around $3300, and we’ve even seen it on sale as low as $2600. Compared to the “Mark II,” the original EOS R5 is surprisingly similar – a tad slower, but still blazing fast, and it has the same 45-megapixel sensor. If I were including older generation cameras in this list, I could easily rank the original EOS R5 right below the Mark II.
Canon EOS R5 Mark II + RF14-35mm F4 L IS USM @ 14mm, ISO 100, 6 seconds, f/16.0

### 5. Sony A7r V
Almost reaching the lofty heights of the Sony A1 II, yet more than $2500 cheaper, is the Sony A7r V. It sells for $4200 (check price) and has an even higher-resolution 61-megapixel sensor.
The A7r V still manages to shoot at 10 FPS despite the high-res sensor, and it has a huge buffer of 583 images. And the autofocus system is incredible: It uses Sony’s newest artificial intelligence, subject-recognition algorithms. Cutting through the buzzwords, this means the A7r V can recognize subjects like birds and people even when they face away from the camera or have an unusual pose.
For a lot of photographers who are considering the Nikon Z9 or Sony A1 II, the A7R V will actually make more sense. It’s an excellent camera for landscape photography because of the high-res sensor, and at 10 FPS, it’s still great for photographing wildlife, too. It doesn’t quite reach the maximum specifications of either the Z9 or A1, but for most applications, it will do just as well as either of those cameras.
Sony A7R III + FE 24-105mm F4 G OSS @ 29mm, ISO 100, 1 second, f/11.0
texts.7:
### 6. Canon EOS R1 and EOS R3
If you want a more specialized camera for sports and wildlife photography, it’s hard to beat the Canon EOS R1, or its little brother the R3. Unlike the previous cameras on this list, the EOS R1 and EOS R3 don’t have a 40+ megapixel sensor; instead, they’re “only” 24 megapixels. But these two cameras can shoot more than 30 FPS with a functionally unlimited buffer. They also have Canon’s unique “eye-sensing autofocus” that begins focusing at the spot _you look at in the composition_. It’s a seriously cool feature.
I paired the two cameras into one entry on this list because they’re surprisingly similar. The main benefits of the EOS R1 are 40 FPS rather than 30 FPS, and a pre-release burst mode. Given that the prices are $6800 and $5400 respectively, I frankly think that a lot of photographers should go with the EOS R3 instead. But if you find pre-release RAW to be worth the extra cash, then of course the flagship EOS R1 has the advantage.
For any fast-paced genres of photography, you’ll want to take a long look at these two cameras. If you don’t need the high-res sensors of the Nikon Z9, Sony A1 II, Sony A7r V, or Canon EOS R5 II, it equals or beats all of them in performance and gives you smaller, more manageable files.
texts.8:
### 7. Sony A7 V
It’s crazy that I haven’t gotten to talk about the Sony A7 V yet – one of the best all-around mirrorless cameras that you can get today, and a great deal, too.
This $2900 camera (check price) has a 33-megapixel sensor, which is a sweet spot for both landscape and wildlife photography. At 30 FPS blackout-free shooting, and borrowing its autofocus system from the Sony A1, it’s an incredible choice for fast-moving action.
Sony has the advantage of being in the full-frame mirrorless market longer than Nikon or Canon, and it’s starting to show now that we’re on the 5th generation of the A7. For example, the large lens lineup for Sony mirrorless cameras (including third-party autofocus lenses) gives you more choices than Canon or Nikon, even though those two companies are catching up.
One of the best “under the radar” features of the Sony A7 V is that it has the redesigned menu system found on Sony’s newest cameras (including the A1 and A7r V). Frankly, Sony’s old menu was a pain to use, even once you got used to it. The new menu makes the camera much more usable.
Sony a7 V + FE 400-800mm F6.3-8 G OSS @ 400mm, ISO 100, 1/250, f/8.0
texts.9:
### 8. Sony A9 III
The Sony A9 III presents entirely new possibilities with its 24-megapixel global shutter. This single innovation completely eliminates rolling shutter and allows flash photography to work at all shutter speeds without high-speed sync.
Due to its new shutter technology, it has an incredible 1/80,000 minimum shutter speed and can shoot at 120fps. It seems very unlikely that anything in the normal world will be too fast for this camera.
At $6000, the Sony A9 III is arguably overpriced, and many of the other cameras here will beat it for other applications – i.e., anything other than sports. This is definitely a highly specialized camera. Still, if you’re aching to use a global shutter, there’s no other camera on this list _but_ the Sony A9III.
Official Sample Shot: the Sony a9III allows flash to be used at all shutter speeds without high-speed sync. ILCE-9M3 + FE 24-70mm F2.8 GM II @ 53mm, ISO 400, 1/6400, f/8.0
texts.10:
### 9. Canon EOS R6 Mark III
Alongside the Sony A7 V, one of the best mirrorless cameras today in terms of price-vs-features is the Canon EOS R6 Mark III. This camera is a replacement for the prior generation EOS R6 Mark II that also remains an excellent choice.
The EOS R6 III has a 32.5-megapixel sensor (compared to 24 megapixels on the previous R6 II).It shoots up to 40 FPS stills, has dual memory card slots, and uses Canon’s superb dual-pixel mirrorless autofocus system. Unlike the previous generation – and unlike most of the other cameras on this list – it’s capable of shooting 7K RAW video.
It does all this at a starting price of $2800. The prior generation EOS R6 Mark II has many of the same features (though a 24 megapixel sensor) and is going on sale for cheap prices these days – about $2000 if it’s on sale.
The EOS R6 Mark III and even the Mark II are practically as good as the Nikon Z9, Sony A1 II, Canon R5 II, and other top cameras where autofocus is concerned. Well done to Canon for putting such a good autofocus system on a less expensive camera. That said, if you’re mainly interested in landscape or studio photography and don’t need so many action photography features, you’d probably happier with one of the other cameras on this list.
Canon EOS R6 + RF800mm F11 IS STM @ 800mm, ISO 1600, 1/1000, f/11.0
texts.11:
### 10. Nikon Z6 III
Nikon has really outdone themselves on the Z6 III, giving this affordable camera essentially the same autofocus system and other features as the top-end Nikon Z9 and Nikon Z8. The main drawback is simply the lower resolution sensor – at 24 megapixels, it’s a little on the low side for today’s world, although still plenty for reasonably sized prints.
The Nikon Z6 III is one of the least expensive ways to get pro-level autofocus and viewfinder performance. As you can see in our comparison of the Nikon Z8 vs the Nikon Z6 III, it even beats the more expensive cameras in a few areas. Not bad for a $2700 camera (and one that often goes on sale for $2300).
NIKON Z6 III + NIKKOR Z 100-400mm f/4.5-5.6 VR S @ 400mm, ISO 180, 1/1000, f/6.3
texts.12:
### 11. Fuji GFX-100S II
One of the most specialized mirrorless cameras today is the Fuji GFX-100S. It’s not a sports or wildlife photography camera at all – instead, it’s a 100-megapixel medium format beast. For landscape photography, architecture, product photography, or other high-resolution needs, it’s probably the best camera on this list. For nonmoving subjects, it even has a sensor-shift mode to quadruple the resolution to 400 megapixels!
My main landscape cameras for years have been the Fuji GFX cameras, and I love them. The lenses, image quality, and dynamic range are amazing, and once you go to medium format, you won’t go back. But because of how specialized this camera is, I don’t think it makes sense to rank the GFX-100S above some of the more practical cameras on this list.
I give a lot of credit to Fuji for releasing the GFX-100S at a reasonable price (for medium format) of $5700. That puts the camera within line of the Nikon Z9 and Sony A1. Even though the GFX-100S is a much slower-paced camera, it has the best sensor of the three.
GFX100S + GF32-64mmF4 R LM WR @ 64mm, ISO 100, 60 seconds, f/16.0. © Meg Faehl
texts.13:
### 12.Fuji GFX-50S II
Pretty much everything that I said about the GFX-100S II above also applies to its little brother, the GFX-50S II. The two cameras share the same design, both have IBIS, and both match each other in most specifications.
However, “most” specifications is not “all” specifications. The GFX-50S II has a 50-megapixel sensor rather than 100-megapixel sensor, and it has a slower contrast-detect autofocus system. The GFX-50S II is also limited to 1080p video for some reason, while the GFX-100S shoots 4K.
Will these differences matter to the typical medium format shooter? Most of them probably won’t, but the sensor resolution might. Considering that the GFX-50S II costs $4000, it’s a pretty stellar deal for medium format. However, if your main reason for getting into this system is maximum detail, you may have a sneaking desire to go with the 100-megapixel version.
GFX 50S + GF32-64mmF4 R LM WR @ 53.6mm, ISO 100, 1/200, f/5.6
texts.14:
### 13. Nikon Z5 II
One of the best values on this entire list is the Nikon Z5 II. Despite being a full-frame camera with plenty of advanced features, including an autofocus system that practically matches that of the Nikon Z8 and Z9, I’ve seen it go as low as $1600 new (check current sales).
You might think that a $1600 full-frame camera (okay, $1850 when it’s not on sale) would have some major flaws, but the Z5 would prove you wrong. Its 24 megapixel sensor is very good, the camera has dual memory card slots, and it still includes in-body image stabilization.
It’s pretty much a “Z6 III lite” and only loses at the margins: 15 FPS rather than 20, a 12-second buffer rather than unlimited, no 6K video, and a less advanced viewfinder. (See the full Z5 II vs Z6 III comparison here.) These are nice features, but none of them are essential to most photographers. If you’re on a budget, it’s hard to beat the Nikon Z5 II – although I will point out that the previous generation Z5 is about the cheapest possible full-frame mirrorless camera, especially if bought used, and it’s a solid camera if you don’t need a top-notch AF system.
NIKON Z 5 + NIKKOR Z 24-200mm f/4-6.3 VR @ 27mm, ISO 100, 1/125, f/8.0
texts.15:
### 14. Nikon Zf
The Nikon Zf is a retro-themed mirrorless camera that pretty much matches the Nikon Z5 II in feature set. The main difference is the design of the camera (and a slightly higher price for the Zf). It’s hard to deny that this is a beautiful camera:
Between the Zf and the Z5 II, the main differences are slightly better battery life on the Zf and slightly better video features on the Z5 II. The price of the Zf is $2200, though – $350 higher than that of the Z5 II, at least when it’s not on sale. It’s probably a camera that you buy more for the ergonomics and beautiful design, while you’d buy the Z5 II if those things are less important than the price. But you can see more at our Zf vs Z5 II comparison to figure out if any of the small differences matter to you.
texts.16:
### 15. Panasonic S5 II
One area where Panasonic had been lagging behind the best mirrorless cameras from Nikon, Canon, and Sony was autofocus performance (at least in Panasonic’s full-frame cameras). The Panasonic S5 II fixes this by introducing the company’s phase-detect AF.
Although the S5 II has a 24-megapixel sensor, don’t let that fool you if you’re a landscape photographer. Like some of the Sony and Fuji cameras on this list, the Panasonic S5 II has a high-resolution pixel-shift mode that quadruples a photo’s resolution to 96 megapixels! This only works if the subject is staying still, but I found that it produces fairly natural results in previous Panasonic mirrorless cameras, like the Panasonic S1R (see our review).
The Panasonic S5 II also has some very good video features, capturing up to 6K video internally. It even has a dedicated cooling fan to allow the camera to keep filming for long stretches without overheating. Add that to the 200-image RAW buffer, the 30 FPS shooting, and the $2000 price, and you have a very versatile mirrorless camera indeed.
DC-S1R + LUMIX S 24-105/F4 @ 105mm, ISO 200, 1/1, f/5.0
texts.17:
### 16. Nikon Z7 II
If you want a high-resolution camera that’s excellent for landscape photography, you should look closely at the 45 megapixel, $3000 Nikon Z7 II.
Even though the Nikon Z7 II isn’t as fast as some other mirrorless cameras – including most of Nikon’s other cameras – it would be one of my top few choices on the market for landscape photography. An unsung feature of the Nikon Z7 II is the base ISO of 64, giving it dynamic range that rivals even medium format! Not to mention that the Z lenses are some of the sharpest lenses of all time, making it an ideal system to capture a lot of detail without weighing very much.
When the Nikon Z7 II was released, it got some bad press for the autofocus system’s wildlife photography capabilities. Of course, it’s all relative: I found that even the previous generation Z7 was perfectly fine for fast wildlife once you get the hang of it. But it’s true that you’d be better served with something like the Canon EOS R5 II, Sony A7r V, or Nikon Z8 if wildlife photography is a priority for you.
NIKON Z 7 II + NIKKOR Z 14-24mm f/2.8 S @ 24mm, ISO 64, 2.5 seconds, f/11.0
texts.18:
### 17. Fujifilm X-T5
I’m a big fan of Fuji’s mirrorless cameras, and the X-T5 has some of the company’s best features so far.
With its 40-megapixel X-Trans sensor capable of producing excellent image quality, in-body image stabilization, a fast X-Processor 4 with Quad CPU that is capable of pushing up 6K video, F-Log gamma for extended dynamic range when shooting video, long battery life, an insanely fast and accurate autofocus system, and a bright 3.69 million dot EVF, the Fuji X-T3 is an impressive stills and video camera. It even shoots 15 FPS (20 FPS if you don’t mind a 1.3x crop), making it a good camera for sports and wildlife, too.
While it is an exceptionally good camera in many ways, it is still an APS-C sensor camera, so it doesn’t do as well at high ISOs or shallow depth of field as the other cameras on this list. It’s also more expensive than most APS-C cameras at $1700 (check price and availability). You may want to consider the prior generation X-T4, too, which I’ve seen go on sale now that the X-T5 is out.
Captured with Fuji X-T4 + XF 23mmF2 R WR @ 23mm, ISO 160, 0.6 sec, f/5.6
texts.19:
### 18. Fujifilm X-H2S
If you want speed in a crop-sensor camera, the Fuji X-H2S is for you. It has a stacked 26MP sensor, which is plenty of resolution for most situations. And it’s _fast_.
Thanks to the camera’s stacked BSI sensor, it can shoot RAW photos at 40 FPS. At that frame rate, your buffer is still a very reasonable 140 images. Drop the burst down to 15 FPS, and you’ll get a 1000-image buffer. So, to say that this camera is good for fast action is an understatement.
The X-H2S also has some very impressive video features with excellent-quality footage – not only with 4K120 but also with 6K 30p. Between this camera and the X-T5 above, I consider the X-T5 more versatile because of its higher-resolution sensor, but the X-H2S isn’t far behind.
texts.20:
### 19. Canon EOS R7
Another fast, APS-C camera that has been turning a lot of heads is the Canon EOS R7. At $1500, it’s about $1000 less expensive than the Fuji X-H2S while nipping at its heels in terms of features.
Those features begin with a 32.5-megapixel sensor, which is high for an APS-C camera. The EOS R7 has a 30 FPS burst, 4K 60p filming, in-body image stabilization, and a great autofocus system. It also has one of my favorite features, a pre-release burst mode that allows you to record photos up to 1/2 second before you’ve fully pressed the shutter button. This is great for unpredictable wildlife photography.
One potential issue is that the buffer is not as big as that of the Fuji X-H2S. The Canon EOS R7 gives you 93 shots at 30 FPS and 187 shots at 15 FPS (assuming that you’re using lossless compressed CRAW). These figures are not low, but not best-in-class either. Even so,the EOS R7 would be one of my first choices for sports and wildlife photography on a budget today.
texts.21:
### 20. Nikon Z50 II
Nikon’s attempt at a high-speed APS-C camera is the Z50 II, and it’s a very good camera in many ways. The autofocus system is borrowed from the flagship Nikon Z9, so it’s a highly capable camera for sports and wildlife photography.
The main downside of this camera is the 20 megapixel resolution – tied for the lowest on this list. 20 megapixels is still plenty for most prints, but it doesn’t leave as much room for cropping, and in today’s world, a lot of people would prefer something over 30 MP just in case they’re making large prints.
Still, the price is good (around $1000) and the features are very impressive. This camera could be an excellent choice depending on your priorities.
NIKON Z50_2 + NIKKOR Z 180-600mm f/5.6-6.3 VR @ 600mm, ISO 25600, 1/250, f/6.3
texts.22:
### 21. Canon EOS R8
This 24-megapixel, full-frame mirrorless camera is aimed at a budget-conscious audience (at least among full-frame cameras) with a price of $1500. It sometimes goes on sale for less; check the current price).
Benefits of the EOS R8 include 40 FPS shooting (electronic shutter) and Canon’s pre-release shutter mode. A drawback of this camera is that it doesn’t have in-body image stabilization, and it has just a single SD card slot. Still, these compromises are what allowed Canon to keep the price of the EOS R8 relatively low. It’s still a great camera with impressive bang for your buck.

For any fast-paced genres of photography, you’ll want to take a long look at these two cameras. If you don’t need the high-res sensors of the Nikon Z9, Sony A1 II, Sony A7r V, or Canon EOS R5 II, it equals or beats all of them in performance and gives you smaller, more manageable files.

### 7. Sony A7 V
It’s crazy that I haven’t gotten to talk about the Sony A7 V yet – one of the best all-around mirrorless cameras that you can get today, and a great deal, too.
This $2900 camera (check price) has a 33-megapixel sensor, which is a sweet spot for both landscape and wildlife photography. At 30 FPS blackout-free shooting, and borrowing its autofocus system from the Sony A1, it’s an incredible choice for fast-moving action.
Sony has the advantage of being in the full-frame mirrorless market longer than Nikon or Canon, and it’s starting to show now that we’re on the 5th generation of the A7. For example, the large lens lineup for Sony mirrorless cameras (including third-party autofocus lenses) gives you more choices than Canon or Nikon, even though those two companies are catching up.
One of the best “under the radar” features of the Sony A7 V is that it has the redesigned menu system found on Sony’s newest cameras (including the A1 and A7r V). Frankly, Sony’s old menu was a pain to use, even once you got used to it. The new menu makes the camera much more usable.
Sony a7 V + FE 400-800mm F6.3-8 G OSS @ 400mm, ISO 100, 1/250, f/8.0

### 8. Sony A9 III
The Sony A9 III presents entirely new possibilities with its 24-megapixel global shutter. This single innovation completely eliminates rolling shutter and allows flash photography to work at all shutter speeds without high-speed sync.
Due to its new shutter technology, it has an incredible 1/80,000 minimum shutter speed and can shoot at 120fps. It seems very unlikely that anything in the normal world will be too fast for this camera.
At $6000, the Sony A9 III is arguably overpriced, and many of the other cameras here will beat it for other applications – i.e., anything other than sports. This is definitely a highly specialized camera. Still, if you’re aching to use a global shutter, there’s no other camera on this list _but_ the Sony A9III.
Official Sample Shot: the Sony a9III allows flash to be used at all shutter speeds without high-speed sync. ILCE-9M3 + FE 24-70mm F2.8 GM II @ 53mm, ISO 400, 1/6400, f/8.0

### 9. Canon EOS R6 Mark III
Alongside the Sony A7 V, one of the best mirrorless cameras today in terms of price-vs-features is the Canon EOS R6 Mark III. This camera is a replacement for the prior generation EOS R6 Mark II that also remains an excellent choice.
The EOS R6 III has a 32.5-megapixel sensor (compared to 24 megapixels on the previous R6 II).It shoots up to 40 FPS stills, has dual memory card slots, and uses Canon’s superb dual-pixel mirrorless autofocus system. Unlike the previous generation – and unlike most of the other cameras on this list – it’s capable of shooting 7K RAW video.
It does all this at a starting price of $2800. The prior generation EOS R6 Mark II has many of the same features (though a 24 megapixel sensor) and is going on sale for cheap prices these days – about $2000 if it’s on sale.
The EOS R6 Mark III and even the Mark II are practically as good as the Nikon Z9, Sony A1 II, Canon R5 II, and other top cameras where autofocus is concerned. Well done to Canon for putting such a good autofocus system on a less expensive camera. That said, if you’re mainly interested in landscape or studio photography and don’t need so many action photography features, you’d probably happier with one of the other cameras on this list.
Canon EOS R6 + RF800mm F11 IS STM @ 800mm, ISO 1600, 1/1000, f/11.0

### 10. Nikon Z6 III
Nikon has really outdone themselves on the Z6 III, giving this affordable camera essentially the same autofocus system and other features as the top-end Nikon Z9 and Nikon Z8. The main drawback is simply the lower resolution sensor – at 24 megapixels, it’s a little on the low side for today’s world, although still plenty for reasonably sized prints.
The Nikon Z6 III is one of the least expensive ways to get pro-level autofocus and viewfinder performance. As you can see in our comparison of the Nikon Z8 vs the Nikon Z6 III, it even beats the more expensive cameras in a few areas. Not bad for a $2700 camera (and one that often goes on sale for $2300).
NIKON Z6 III + NIKKOR Z 100-400mm f/4.5-5.6 VR S @ 400mm, ISO 180, 1/1000, f/6.3

### 11. Fuji GFX-100S II
One of the most specialized mirrorless cameras today is the Fuji GFX-100S. It’s not a sports or wildlife photography camera at all – instead, it’s a 100-megapixel medium format beast. For landscape photography, architecture, product photography, or other high-resolution needs, it’s probably the best camera on this list. For nonmoving subjects, it even has a sensor-shift mode to quadruple the resolution to 400 megapixels!
My main landscape cameras for years have been the Fuji GFX cameras, and I love them. The lenses, image quality, and dynamic range are amazing, and once you go to medium format, you won’t go back. But because of how specialized this camera is, I don’t think it makes sense to rank the GFX-100S above some of the more practical cameras on this list.
I give a lot of credit to Fuji for releasing the GFX-100S at a reasonable price (for medium format) of $5700. That puts the camera within line of the Nikon Z9 and Sony A1. Even though the GFX-100S is a much slower-paced camera, it has the best sensor of the three.
GFX100S + GF32-64mmF4 R LM WR @ 64mm, ISO 100, 60 seconds, f/16.0. © Meg Faehl

### 12.Fuji GFX-50S II
Pretty much everything that I said about the GFX-100S II above also applies to its little brother, the GFX-50S II. The two cameras share the same design, both have IBIS, and both match each other in most specifications.
However, “most” specifications is not “all” specifications. The GFX-50S II has a 50-megapixel sensor rather than 100-megapixel sensor, and it has a slower contrast-detect autofocus system. The GFX-50S II is also limited to 1080p video for some reason, while the GFX-100S shoots 4K.
Will these differences matter to the typical medium format shooter? Most of them probably won’t, but the sensor resolution might. Considering that the GFX-50S II costs $4000, it’s a pretty stellar deal for medium format. However, if your main reason for getting into this system is maximum detail, you may have a sneaking desire to go with the 100-megapixel version.
GFX 50S + GF32-64mmF4 R LM WR @ 53.6mm, ISO 100, 1/200, f/5.6

### 13. Nikon Z5 II
One of the best values on this entire list is the Nikon Z5 II. Despite being a full-frame camera with plenty of advanced features, including an autofocus system that practically matches that of the Nikon Z8 and Z9, I’ve seen it go as low as $1600 new (check current sales).
You might think that a $1600 full-frame camera (okay, $1850 when it’s not on sale) would have some major flaws, but the Z5 would prove you wrong. Its 24 megapixel sensor is very good, the camera has dual memory card slots, and it still includes in-body image stabilization.
It’s pretty much a “Z6 III lite” and only loses at the margins: 15 FPS rather than 20, a 12-second buffer rather than unlimited, no 6K video, and a less advanced viewfinder. (See the full Z5 II vs Z6 III comparison here.) These are nice features, but none of them are essential to most photographers. If you’re on a budget, it’s hard to beat the Nikon Z5 II – although I will point out that the previous generation Z5 is about the cheapest possible full-frame mirrorless camera, especially if bought used, and it’s a solid camera if you don’t need a top-notch AF system.
NIKON Z 5 + NIKKOR Z 24-200mm f/4-6.3 VR @ 27mm, ISO 100, 1/125, f/8.0

### 14. Nikon Zf
The Nikon Zf is a retro-themed mirrorless camera that pretty much matches the Nikon Z5 II in feature set. The main difference is the design of the camera (and a slightly higher price for the Zf). It’s hard to deny that this is a beautiful camera:
Between the Zf and the Z5 II, the main differences are slightly better battery life on the Zf and slightly better video features on the Z5 II. The price of the Zf is $2200, though – $350 higher than that of the Z5 II, at least when it’s not on sale. It’s probably a camera that you buy more for the ergonomics and beautiful design, while you’d buy the Z5 II if those things are less important than the price. But you can see more at our Zf vs Z5 II comparison to figure out if any of the small differences matter to you.

### 15. Panasonic S5 II
One area where Panasonic had been lagging behind the best mirrorless cameras from Nikon, Canon, and Sony was autofocus performance (at least in Panasonic’s full-frame cameras). The Panasonic S5 II fixes this by introducing the company’s phase-detect AF.
Although the S5 II has a 24-megapixel sensor, don’t let that fool you if you’re a landscape photographer. Like some of the Sony and Fuji cameras on this list, the Panasonic S5 II has a high-resolution pixel-shift mode that quadruples a photo’s resolution to 96 megapixels! This only works if the subject is staying still, but I found that it produces fairly natural results in previous Panasonic mirrorless cameras, like the Panasonic S1R (see our review).
The Panasonic S5 II also has some very good video features, capturing up to 6K video internally. It even has a dedicated cooling fan to allow the camera to keep filming for long stretches without overheating. Add that to the 200-image RAW buffer, the 30 FPS shooting, and the $2000 price, and you have a very versatile mirrorless camera indeed.
DC-S1R + LUMIX S 24-105/F4 @ 105mm, ISO 200, 1/1, f/5.0

### 16. Nikon Z7 II
If you want a high-resolution camera that’s excellent for landscape photography, you should look closely at the 45 megapixel, $3000 Nikon Z7 II.
Even though the Nikon Z7 II isn’t as fast as some other mirrorless cameras – including most of Nikon’s other cameras – it would be one of my top few choices on the market for landscape photography. An unsung feature of the Nikon Z7 II is the base ISO of 64, giving it dynamic range that rivals even medium format! Not to mention that the Z lenses are some of the sharpest lenses of all time, making it an ideal system to capture a lot of detail without weighing very much.
When the Nikon Z7 II was released, it got some bad press for the autofocus system’s wildlife photography capabilities. Of course, it’s all relative: I found that even the previous generation Z7 was perfectly fine for fast wildlife once you get the hang of it. But it’s true that you’d be better served with something like the Canon EOS R5 II, Sony A7r V, or Nikon Z8 if wildlife photography is a priority for you.
NIKON Z 7 II + NIKKOR Z 14-24mm f/2.8 S @ 24mm, ISO 64, 2.5 seconds, f/11.0

### 17. Fujifilm X-T5
I’m a big fan of Fuji’s mirrorless cameras, and the X-T5 has some of the company’s best features so far.
With its 40-megapixel X-Trans sensor capable of producing excellent image quality, in-body image stabilization, a fast X-Processor 4 with Quad CPU that is capable of pushing up 6K video, F-Log gamma for extended dynamic range when shooting video, long battery life, an insanely fast and accurate autofocus system, and a bright 3.69 million dot EVF, the Fuji X-T3 is an impressive stills and video camera. It even shoots 15 FPS (20 FPS if you don’t mind a 1.3x crop), making it a good camera for sports and wildlife, too.
While it is an exceptionally good camera in many ways, it is still an APS-C sensor camera, so it doesn’t do as well at high ISOs or shallow depth of field as the other cameras on this list. It’s also more expensive than most APS-C cameras at $1700 (check price and availability). You may want to consider the prior generation X-T4, too, which I’ve seen go on sale now that the X-T5 is out.
Captured with Fuji X-T4 + XF 23mmF2 R WR @ 23mm, ISO 160, 0.6 sec, f/5.6

### 18. Fujifilm X-H2S
If you want speed in a crop-sensor camera, the Fuji X-H2S is for you. It has a stacked 26MP sensor, which is plenty of resolution for most situations. And it’s _fast_.
Thanks to the camera’s stacked BSI sensor, it can shoot RAW photos at 40 FPS. At that frame rate, your buffer is still a very reasonable 140 images. Drop the burst down to 15 FPS, and you’ll get a 1000-image buffer. So, to say that this camera is good for fast action is an understatement.
The X-H2S also has some very impressive video features with excellent-quality footage – not only with 4K120 but also with 6K 30p. Between this camera and the X-T5 above, I consider the X-T5 more versatile because of its higher-resolution sensor, but the X-H2S isn’t far behind.

### 19. Canon EOS R7
Another fast, APS-C camera that has been turning a lot of heads is the Canon EOS R7. At $1500, it’s about $1000 less expensive than the Fuji X-H2S while nipping at its heels in terms of features.
Those features begin with a 32.5-megapixel sensor, which is high for an APS-C camera. The EOS R7 has a 30 FPS burst, 4K 60p filming, in-body image stabilization, and a great autofocus system. It also has one of my favorite features, a pre-release burst mode that allows you to record photos up to 1/2 second before you’ve fully pressed the shutter button. This is great for unpredictable wildlife photography.
One potential issue is that the buffer is not as big as that of the Fuji X-H2S. The Canon EOS R7 gives you 93 shots at 30 FPS and 187 shots at 15 FPS (assuming that you’re using lossless compressed CRAW). These figures are not low, but not best-in-class either. Even so,the EOS R7 would be one of my first choices for sports and wildlife photography on a budget today.

### 20. Nikon Z50 II
Nikon’s attempt at a high-speed APS-C camera is the Z50 II, and it’s a very good camera in many ways. The autofocus system is borrowed from the flagship Nikon Z9, so it’s a highly capable camera for sports and wildlife photography.
The main downside of this camera is the 20 megapixel resolution – tied for the lowest on this list. 20 megapixels is still plenty for most prints, but it doesn’t leave as much room for cropping, and in today’s world, a lot of people would prefer something over 30 MP just in case they’re making large prints.
Still, the price is good (around $1000) and the features are very impressive. This camera could be an excellent choice depending on your priorities.
NIKON Z50_2 + NIKKOR Z 180-600mm f/5.6-6.3 VR @ 600mm, ISO 25600, 1/250, f/6.3

### 21. Canon EOS R8
This 24-megapixel, full-frame mirrorless camera is aimed at a budget-conscious audience (at least among full-frame cameras) with a price of $1500. It sometimes goes on sale for less; check the current price).
Benefits of the EOS R8 include 40 FPS shooting (electronic shutter) and Canon’s pre-release shutter mode. A drawback of this camera is that it doesn’t have in-body image stabilization, and it has just a single SD card slot. Still, these compromises are what allowed Canon to keep the price of the EOS R8 relatively low. It’s still a great camera with impressive bang for your buck.

### Best Mirrorless Camera
The Fujifilm X-T5 packs the 40 Megapixel sensor and built-in stabilisation from the flagship X-H2 into a slightly smaller and lighter version of the X-T4 with the screen articulation of the X-T3. Impressively it’s only 18g heavier than the X-T3 while sporting the bigger battery and IBIS unit both lacking from that model. As such it’s literally the camera many of the Fuji-faithful have been waiting for, with a feature-set and design-aesthetic cherry-picked for photographers, without getting bogged down by the technical demands of videographers or action shooters. Fujifilm’s message is clear: if you want their top performance, especially for bursts and video, along with accessories including a battery grip, then spend $300 more on the X-H2 and forgo the retro chic. If you simply want the X-H2’s pure photo quality in a slightly smaller and lighter body with the classic X-T exposure dials, and a screen that tilts rather than flips, then the X-T5 is the camera for you. If however you want the full X-H2 performance in an X-T body with an optional grip, you’re out of luck. Ultimately the X-T may remain high-end, but is no longer the flagship that has to please everyone in terms of performance and features. I feel Fujifilm has made sensible choices on what to include and what to miss out. As such the X-T5 is the perfect upgrade for owners of the X-T1, 2 and 3, not to mention a compelling entry for those new to the system. I loved shooting with it, and guess what, it’s not bad at video either.
Check prices on the Fujifilm X-T5 at B&H, Adorama, WEX UK or Calumet.de. Alternatively get yourself a copy of my In Camera book, an official Cameralabs T-shirt or mug, or treat me to a coffee! Thanks!

The A7 IV may be classified as the entry-level model in Sony’s full-frame lineup, but like its predecessors, will more than satisfy the majority of photographers, videographers and hybrid shooters. The Mark IV boosts the resolution to 33 Megapixels without compromising noise levels, enhances an already excellent autofocus system, improves the menus and controls, increases the viewfinder resolution and sports a more comfortable grip. There’s also support for new flashguns with greater communications via the multi-interface shoe. The top burst speed remains 10fps, but reduces when shooting RAW to 8 or even 6fps depending on compression and there still no focus bracketing or bulb timers. Meanwhile videographers get 10 bit, 4k at 50 or 60p (albeit with a 1.5x crop), a flip screen, active stabilization, gyro data, some cool focus tools, and the ability to record clips longer than 30mins without overheating. It’ll even work as a standard USB webcam. If you want RAW video, uncropped 4k at 60 or even 120p, less skewing, and faster RAW bursts, then you should weigh-up the features of the Canon R6, Lumix S5 and Lumix GH6 to name but three. But while the A7 IV has a handful of annoyances, the pros overwhelmingly add up to an extremely capable
camera  
. In terms of an all-rounder, the A7 IV becomes the one to beat and comes Highly Recommended.

Mirrorless cameras have effectively become the industry standard. As a result, DSLR prices keep falling, which can make them tempting, and you certainly don't need cutting-edge gear to take great photos or enjoy the hobby. DSLRs can even be some of the best cameras for beginners. Still, if you want access to the latest camera technology, both now and in the years ahead, a mirrorless model is the smarter buy.
Mirrorless cameras also have a few practical advantages. They're usually smaller and lighter than DSLRs, their autofocus systems are faster and more precise, and their electronic viewfinders show you exactly how your exposure will look before you press the shutter. The category has grown quickly, too, so you'll find options for nearly every budget and skill level.
When choosing one, start with the lens mount, since you'll likely keep buying into that system for years. Then think about sensor size. Full-frame models like our top two picks have an edge in low light, while APS-C and Micro Four Thirds cameras keep both bodies and lenses more compact and affordable.
We've bought and tested over 135 cameras, and below, you'll find the best mirrorless camera to buy. If you want a full-frame body specifically, see our best full-frame mirrorless camera picks. First-time buyers may find a better fit in our best mirrorless cameras for beginners or best budget mirrorless cameras articles. For a broader look that includes DSLRs and fixed-lens models, check out our best digital cameras.

Its sensor delivers fast, blackout-free RAW bursts and excellent image quality, backed by Sony's extensive E-mount lens lineup. Its 33-megapixel resolution carries over from the previous generation, the Sony α7 IV, but the sensor behind it is now partially stacked. This gives it much faster readouts, which, with the electronic shutter, enables it to capture full 14-bit RAW files at up to 30 fps without viewfinder blackout, and rolling shutter distortion drops noticeably. Pre-capture kicks in as soon as you half-press the shutter button, saving the second of action before you fully press it. Its autofocus tracks people, animals, and vehicles during those bursts, even if it can sometimes lose its target. In our tests, it delivered excellent RAW image quality, with crisp detail, exceptional dynamic range, and clean results in low light.

Handling holds up just as well; the handgrip is deep and large enough to comfortably fit all your fingers, and there's a rear rest that should suit most hand sizes, making the camera comfortable to use for long periods and balanced, even with larger lenses. The body is weather-sealed, the battery outlasts most of the competition, and the screen can tilt for low angles or flip to the side to face you. Sony's E-mount also gives it a lasting edge. No other system has as many native and third-party lenses across every budget, which matters more over the life of a camera than any single spec. ## How to Choose: Pick the System Before the Camera
You’ll probably replace your camera body in a few years. The lenses can stay with you for a lot longer than that, and they only fit one maker’s mount. So the bigger decision is the system you’re buying into, and the body comes second.
I’ve been a Canon user since I was 13, and that’s how it’s worked out for me. When I moved from the Canon 6D to the R5, I didn’t have to replace a single lens. It cost me an adapter rather than a new bag of glass, which is about the cheapest upgrade a photographer ever gets to make.

## How to Choose: Pick the System Before the Camera
### Which Mounts Are Open to Other Lens Makers?
Third-party lenses from the likes of Sigma, Tamron and Viltrox are often cheaper than the camera maker’s own, and some fill gaps in the range. How many you can choose from depends a lot on the mount:
*   Sony E-mount is the most open of the big systems. Sony released its specifications to other lens makers royalty-free back in 2011, and it has the widest choice of third-party full-frame autofocus lenses. Some Sony bodies do limit burst speed with some third-party lenses.  
*   Fujifilm opened its X-mount to third parties in 2020, and you can now buy autofocus X lenses from Sigma, Tamron, Viltrox, Tokina and Zeiss.  
*   Nikon’s Z-mount is partly open. Tamron, Laowa and Viltrox make full-frame autofocus lenses for it, while Sigma’s Z lenses are APS-C only.  
*   Canon’s RF mount is the most restricted for full-frame. Sigma and Tamron have sold Canon-licensed autofocus RF lenses since April 2024, but almost all of them are APS-C (RF-S) lenses, and the full-frame third-party options tend to be manual focus. If you’re buying a full-frame Canon, budget for Canon’s own lenses.  
*   The L-mount was set up as an alliance by Leica, Panasonic and Sigma in 2018, and other members have joined since. If you buy a Panasonic Lumix S body, Sigma’s L-mount lenses fit it natively, with no adapter.
In practice, it means a beginner buying a Canon APS-C body like the R10 has plenty of affordable lens options, while someone buying a Canon full-frame body is mostly paying Canon prices for glass.

## How to Choose: Pick the System Before the Camera
### What a First Kit Costs Beyond the Body
The price on the box is never the price of the kit. Before you settle on a body, add up what you’ll actually need to go out and shoot:
*   A lens. The kit lens is fine to start with, but the next lens you buy (usually a fast prime or a telephoto zoom) can easily cost as much as an entry-level body. Our guide to the best lenses for travel photography covers what to buy next.  
*   A spare battery. Mirrorless cameras run their screen or electronic viewfinder the whole time they’re on, so they get through batteries faster than DSLRs, and even faster in the cold (my cold weather photography tips cover that). Carry at least one spare.  
*   The right memory card. Check which card type the body takes before you buy, because some higher-end cameras need CFexpress cards, which cost a lot more than SD cards.
If the total is over your budget, drop a tier on the body before you skimp on the lens.

## How to Choose: Pick the System Before the Camera
### Already Own DSLR Lenses?
Then the brand decision has probably been made for you. All three of the big DSLR makers sell an adapter that lets your old lenses work on their mirrorless bodies:
*   Canon’s EF-EOS R mount adapter lets EF and EF-S lenses work on Canon’s RF bodies, and Canon says there’s no loss of autofocus speed or image stabilisation. It’s how every lens I own goes on my R5, and it’s dust- and water-resistant too. It’s $149.00 In Stock on Amazon, and Canon also makes a version with a control ring.  
*   Nikon’s FTZ II adapter puts F-mount lenses on Z bodies. You get full autofocus with AF-S, AF-P and AF-I lenses, while older screw-drive AF-D lenses become manual focus.  
*   Sony’s LA-EA5 adapts A-mount lenses to E-mount bodies, but autofocus with older screw-drive lenses only works on some recent Sony bodies, so check Sony’s compatibility list for yours before you rely on it.
If you’ve got a good set of DSLR lenses, the adapter is the cheapest part of switching to mirrorless. Our DSLR beginner’s guide is still worth a read if you’re sticking with the camera you have for now.

## How to Choose: Pick the System Before the Camera
### Best Enthusiast Full-Frame: Nikon Z6 III
Already in Nikon’s system and want one body to do everything? Get the Nikon Z6 III.
It uses a 24.5MP partially-stacked sensor, which Nikon says reads out about 3.5 times faster than the conventional sensor in the Z6 II. That speed is behind its fast electronic shutter and quick bursts. Nikon rates the in-body stabilisation at up to 8 stops, it records 6K/60p RAW video internally, and Nikon says the body has the same level of dust and drip resistance as its professional Z8, rated to work down to -10°C.
If you own Nikon F-mount lenses, the FTZ II adapter puts them on the Z6 III with full autofocus, as long as they’re AF-S, AF-P or AF-I lenses. Older screw-drive lenses work in manual focus only.
At 760g with battery and card, it’s the heaviest camera on this list, so look elsewhere if weight is your main concern.
**Pros:** fast partially-stacked sensor, 8-stop stabilisation, internal 6K RAW, Z8-level sealing.
**Cons:** the heaviest body here, and fewer third-party full-frame lenses than Sony.
**Key specs**
*   Sensor: 24.5MP full-frame, partially stacked  
*   Stabilisation: in-body, up to 8 stops  
*   Weight: 760g with battery and card  
*   Video: 6K/60p internal RAW  
*   Mount: Nikon Z
**Best for:** Nikon shooters who want a do-everything full-frame body.
**Check price on Amazon and B&H**

## How to Choose: Pick the System Before the Camera
### Best Sony Full-Frame All-Rounder: Sony a7 V
Sony calls the a7 V an all-around full-frame camera. It sits below the Alpha 1 II, Sony’s flagship, and above the smaller a7C II.
It has a 33MP sensor, in-body stabilisation and Sony’s AI-based subject recognition, and it shoots bursts of up to 30fps. Sony says the body is designed with dust and drip resistance in mind, and also says it won’t completely keep dust and water out.
The choice between this and the a7C II is mostly about handling. The a7 V is heavier at 695g, but it has the bigger grip and more of the physical controls you’ll use every day. If you don’t need the smallest Sony, just get the a7 V.
**Pros:** fast, dependable autofocus, quick bursts, better handling than the a7C II, the most open lens mount.
**Cons:** heavier and pricier than the a7C II.
**Key specs**
*   Sensor: 33MP full-frame  
*   Stabilisation: in-body, sensor-shift  
*   Weight: 695g with battery and card  
*   Mount: Sony E
**Best for:** Sony shooters who want one full-frame body for everything.
**Check price on Amazon and B&H**

## How to Choose: Pick the System Before the Camera
### Best for Video: Canon EOS R6 V
If video is the main reason you’re buying, start with the Canon EOS R6 V. Canon calls it a video-centric camera.
It records 7K RAW at 60p from a 32.5MP full-frame sensor, and a built-in cooling fan keeps it going on long takes. Canon quotes up to 120 minutes of continuous 7K 60p RAW Light or uncropped 4K 60p recording (measured at 23°C from a cold start), so in normal conditions overheating shouldn’t cut a long take short. For takes that long you’ll want external power, as Canon rates a single battery at about 70 minutes of 4K 60p. Stabilisation is rated at 7.5 stops in the centre.
There’s no electronic viewfinder, though, so you compose on the rear screen. There’s no mechanical shutter either, only an electronic one (up to 1/16000s), and Canon itself warns that fast-moving subjects can show rolling-shutter distortion.
Canon says flash support with the electronic shutter is coming in a future firmware update. For stills, buy the R6 Mark III instead. The R6 V doesn’t replace it, and Canon sells the two side by side.
If you want one camera that does video and stills well, the Panasonic Lumix S5 II is the better hybrid. It has a viewfinder, and Panasonic says it records unlimited 4K (C4K and 4K at up to 60p, as long as you’re between 0 and 40°C). It uses the L-mount, so Sigma’s lenses are an option too. I’d only choose the R6 V over the S5 II if video clearly comes first for you.
**Pros:** 7K RAW, long recording times with the fan, strong stabilisation.
**Cons:** no viewfinder, no mechanical shutter, and not a camera I’d buy for stills.
**Key specs**

**Best for:** video-first shooters and content creators who want long recording times.
**Check price on Amazon and B&H**

## How to Choose: Pick the System Before the Camera
### Best for Wildlife and Action: Canon EOS R7
The Canon EOS R7 is my pick for wildlife on a budget. It’s Canon’s top APS-C body, and for wildlife the smaller sensor works in your favour.
On my R5, the EF 100-400mm is my wildlife lens. Put the same lens on an R7 and the 1.6x crop makes it frame like a 160-640mm, so distant animals fill quite a lot more of the frame without you buying a longer lens. It also takes EF lenses through the same adapter I use, which makes it a natural second body for anyone with Canon DSLR glass.
It shoots 15fps with the mechanical shutter and up to 30fps with the electronic one, Canon rates the stabilisation at up to 7 stops, and Canon describes the body as dust and moisture resistant, a claim it doesn’t make for the R10.
It’s been around since 2022, and as of November 2026, Canon hasn’t announced a successor.
**Pros:** extra reach from the crop sensor, fast bursts, sealed body, works with EF lenses on the adapter.
**Cons:** an older design than most of this list, and APS-C struggles more than full-frame in low light at dawn and dusk.

*   Sensor: 32.5MP APS-C  
*   Stabilisation: in-body, up to 7 stops  
*   Weight: 612g with battery and card  
*   Burst: 15fps mechanical, 30fps electronic  
*   Mount: Canon RF
**Best for:** wildlife, birds and sport, on a budget.
**Check price on Amazon and B&H**

## How to Choose: Pick the System Before the Camera
### Best Sony APS-C: Sony a6700
The Sony a6700 is my favourite of Sony’s APS-C cameras, mostly for its autofocus. That’s also why it tops my travel camera guide.
You get a 26MP sensor, sensor-shift stabilisation and Sony’s subject-tracking autofocus in a body that weighs 493g with battery and card. Sony’s E-mount also gives you more lens choice than any other APS-C system, including affordable options from Sigma and Tamron.
The main downside is Sony’s menu system. It’s improved over the years, but it’s still a bit harder to find your way around than Canon’s or Fujifilm’s. If you’re the sort of person who sets a camera up once and leaves it, that won’t bother you much.
**Pros:** fast, reliable autofocus, small and light, lots of lens choice.
**Cons:** fiddly menus, fewer physical controls than the X-T5.
**Key specs**
*   Sensor: 26MP APS-C  
*   Stabilisation: in-body, sensor-shift  
*   Weight: 493g with battery and card  
*   Mount: Sony E
**Best for:** anyone who shoots moving subjects and wants a small camera.
**Check price on Amazon and B&H**

If video is the main reason you’re buying, start with the Canon EOS R6 V. Canon calls it a video-centric camera.
It records 7K RAW at 60p from a 32.5MP full-frame sensor, and a built-in cooling fan keeps it going on long takes. Canon quotes up to 120 minutes of continuous 7K 60p RAW Light or uncropped 4K 60p recording (measured at 23°C from a cold start), so in normal conditions overheating shouldn’t cut a long take short. For takes that long you’ll want external power, as Canon rates a single battery at about 70 minutes of 4K 60p. Stabilisation is rated at 7.5 stops in the centre.
There’s no electronic viewfinder, though, so you compose on the rear screen. There’s no mechanical shutter either, only an electronic one (up to 1/16000s), and Canon itself warns that fast-moving subjects can show rolling-shutter distortion.
Canon says flash support with the electronic shutter is coming in a future firmware update. For stills, buy the R6 Mark III instead. The R6 V doesn’t replace it, and Canon sells the two side by side.
If you want one camera that does video and stills well, the Panasonic Lumix S5 II is the better hybrid. It has a viewfinder, and Panasonic says it records unlimited 4K (C4K and 4K at up to 60p, as long as you’re between 0 and 40°C). It uses the L-mount, so Sigma’s lenses are an option too. I’d only choose the R6 V over the S5 II if video clearly comes first for you.
**Pros:** 7K RAW, long recording times with the fan, strong stabilisation.
**Cons:** no viewfinder, no mechanical shutter, and not a camera I’d buy for stills.

Mirrorless cameras have effectively become the industry standard. As a result, DSLR prices keep falling, which can make them tempting, and you certainly don't need cutting-edge gear to take great photos or enjoy the hobby. DSLRs can even be some of the best cameras for beginners. Still, if you want access to the latest camera technology, both now and in the years ahead, a mirrorless model is the smarter buy.
Mirrorless cameras also have a few practical advantages. They're usually smaller and lighter than DSLRs, their autofocus systems are faster and more precise, and their electronic viewfinders show you exactly how your exposure will look before you press the shutter. The category has grown quickly, too, so you'll find options for nearly every budget and skill level.
When choosing one, start with the lens mount, since you'll likely keep buying into that system for years. Then think about sensor size. Full-frame models like our top two picks have an edge in low light, while APS-C and Micro Four Thirds cameras keep both bodies and lenses more compact and affordable.
We've bought and tested over 135 cameras, and below, you'll find the best mirrorless camera to buy. If you want a full-frame body specifically, see our best full-frame mirrorless camera picks. ## How to Choose: Pick the System Before the Camera
You’ll probably replace your camera body in a few years. The lenses can stay with you for a lot longer than that, and they only fit one maker’s mount. So the bigger decision is the system you’re buying into, and the body comes second.
I’ve been a Canon user since I was 13, and that’s how it’s worked out for me. When I moved from the Canon 6D to the R5, I didn’t have to replace a single lens. It cost me an adapter rather than a new bag of glass, which is about the cheapest upgrade a photographer ever gets to make.

## How to Choose: Pick the System Before the Camera
### Which Mounts Are Open to Other Lens Makers?
Third-party lenses from the likes of Sigma, Tamron and Viltrox are often cheaper than the camera maker’s own, and some fill gaps in the range. How many you can choose from depends a lot on the mount:
*   Sony E-mount is the most open of the big systems. Sony released its specifications to other lens makers royalty-free back in 2011, and it has the widest choice of third-party full-frame autofocus lenses. Some Sony bodies do limit burst speed with some third-party lenses.  
*   Fujifilm opened its X-mount to third parties in 2020, and you can now buy autofocus X lenses from Sigma, Tamron, Viltrox, Tokina and Zeiss.  
*   Nikon’s Z-mount is partly open. Tamron, Laowa and Viltrox make full-frame autofocus lenses for it, while Sigma’s Z lenses are APS-C only.  
*   Canon’s RF mount is the most restricted for full-frame. Sigma and Tamron have sold Canon-licensed autofocus RF lenses since April 2024, but almost all of them are APS-C (RF-S) lenses, and the full-frame third-party options tend to be manual focus. If you’re buying a full-frame Canon, budget for Canon’s own lenses.  
*   The L-mount was set up as an alliance by Leica, Panasonic and Sigma in 2018, and other members have joined since. If you buy a Panasonic Lumix S body, Sigma’s L-mount lenses fit it natively, with no adapter.
In practice, it means a beginner buying a Canon APS-C body like the R10 has plenty of affordable lens options, while someone buying a Canon full-frame body is mostly paying Canon prices for glass.

The price on the box is never the price of the kit. Before you settle on a body, add up what you’ll actually need to go out and shoot:
*   A lens. The kit lens is fine to start with, but the next lens you buy (usually a fast prime or a telephoto zoom) can easily cost as much as an entry-level body. Our guide to the best lenses for travel photography covers what to buy next.  
*   A spare battery. Mirrorless cameras run their screen or electronic viewfinder the whole time they’re on, so they get through batteries faster than DSLRs, and even faster in the cold (my cold weather photography tips cover that). Carry at least one spare.  
*   The right memory card. Check which card type the body takes before you buy, because some higher-end cameras need CFexpress cards, which cost a lot more than SD cards.
If the total is over your budget, drop a tier on the body before you skimp on the lens.

Then the brand decision has probably been made for you. All three of the big DSLR makers sell an adapter that lets your old lenses work on their mirrorless bodies:
*   Canon’s EF-EOS R mount adapter lets EF and EF-S lenses work on Canon’s RF bodies, and Canon says there’s no loss of autofocus speed or image stabilisation. *   Nikon’s FTZ II adapter puts F-mount lenses on Z bodies. You get full autofocus with AF-S, AF-P and AF-I lenses, while older screw-drive AF-D lenses become manual focus.  
*   Sony’s LA-EA5 adapts A-mount lenses to E-mount bodies, but autofocus with older screw-drive lenses only works on some recent Sony bodies, so check Sony’s compatibility list for yours before you rely on it.

### Best Mirrorless Camera
The EOS R6 Mark II addresses a number of issues with the original model to become one of the most powerful all-round cameras in its peer group. Most notably it now shoots much faster than the Sony A7 IV, sports broader and more confident subject recognition in my tests, while its ability to film uncropped, oversampled 4k video up to 60p is a key advantage, and unlike the original R6, it never overheated in my tests. Plus you’re getting focus bracketing and stacking in-camera, Bulb timers, multiple exposures and slightly better stabilisation. Of all the upgrades, Auto subject detection is arguably the most useful in day-to-day use, figuring out if you’re pointing the camera at people, birds, animals or vehicles with a high success rate. Meanwhile the A7 IV fights back with higher resolution files and the ability to use a huge array of third party lenses including models from Sigma and Tamron. Then there’s the Lumix S5 II which sports a pixel-shift mode, a wealth of pro-level video-centric features, third-party
lens  
support from Sigma, and a significant price saving too. Indeed body price and choice of native lenses are the main issues facing the R6 II. Ultimately the R6 II, A7 IV and S5 II are all excellent cameras most of us would be delighted to own. Choosing one involves weighing up body price, lens availability and drilling-down to specific features you may or may not need. If your budget will stretch and you’re happy to use Canon’s own lenses, I can Highly Recommend the R6 II as an all-rounder, and especially for anyone photographing sports or wildlife, but if you’re not wedded to the company, do compare it closely to rivals.

### Best Mirrorless Camera
The Lumix S5 Mark II is arguably the best value new full-frame camera around at the time of making this review, packing a wealth of features while comfortably undercutting key rivals on price. The long-awaited inclusion of phase-detect autofocus transforms both photo and video, eliminating the distracting pulsing which haunted earlier Lumix cameras. While the core features and specs are roughly similar to its rivals, drilling-down reveals unique benefits to each: Canon’s R6 II enjoyed the best subject detection in my tests, allows uncropped 4k up to 60p, in-camera focus stacking, multiple exposures, a bulb timer, pre-capture mode, 1080 180p slow motion, and the fastest mechanical burst speed of 12fps. Sony’s A7 IV has the highest resolution on a single frame, support for a faster memory card and access to a wealth of lenses including Tamron’s which aren’t yet available for L or RF mount. Meanwhile the S5 II boasts a high-res pixel shift mode, focus bracketing with a mechanical shutter that allows flash, open-gate 6k video, waveform and vector displays, anamorphic modes, real-time LUT previews, and potentially longer recording times under hotter conditions thanks to a built-in fan. And don’t forget Sigma’s growing series of excellent DG DN lenses is available for both e and L-mounts, giving Sony and Panasonic access to affordable third-party lenses that Canon owners can currently only dream of. Oh, and there’s that $500 or pound saving over the R6 II and A7 IV. In fact it still undercuts their body prices when sold in a twin lens kit with the 20-60 and 50 1.8. Of course both Canon and Sony still sell their previous versions at prices closer to the S5 II, but their feature-sets aren’t as complete. If you’re mostly shooting action or wildlife I’d say it’s worth spending the extra on the R6 II, but as an all-round hybrid
camera  
for a general mix of photo and video, the Lumix S5 II is simply hard to beat at the price and comes Highly Recommended.
